summary: The article describes a resurgence of home canning, pickling, and family recipe preservation after September 1, 2023, framing it as both sustainability practice and cultural preservation. It profiles families, workshops, community kitchens, fishermen, and farmers who use preservation to cut food waste, energy use, and packaging. It concludes that preserving food and recipes honors heritage while protecting the environment.
one_line: A 2023 resurgence in canning, pickling, and recipe archiving is portrayed as a sustainable way to preserve food, family heritage, and the environment.
key_facts: Roberta Robinson of Montana is a third-generation canner; the family tradition began with her grandmother in autumn 1942, when she canned out of necessity during the war.
Home economist Jamie Elliot says canning your own produce reduces the carbon footprint by minimizing industrial processing and long-distance transportation.
Chris Matheson's 'Pickling Workshops' in Portland, Maine had waiting lists stretching into the new year by September 15, 2023.
Pickling uses vegetables and fruits that might otherwise go to waste, which the article frames as a stand against throwaway culture.
The Heritage Recipe Archive was founded on October 3, 2023, by siblings Sarah and Alex Johnson to digitally preserve family recipes.
Sarah Johnson says her grandparents cooked without harming the environment, used every part of a plant or animal, and knew what grew best and when.
Since September 22, 2023, the Central Community Kitchen in Atlanta, Georgia, directed by chef Michael Thompson, has hosted canning and pickling circles.
Community canning groups reduce environmental impact through bulk purchasing of ingredients, sharing equipment, and learning waste-reducing techniques.
Fisherman Jeremiah Huang started the Sustainable Seas Co-op in the Pacific Northwest on September 29, 2023, promoting canning of locally caught fish for a year-round supply.
Huang says canning fish during high season reduces strain on marine populations.
Emily Chastain of Vermont farms with the intention of preserving, a practice she has followed since late September 2023.
Farms selling preserved goods create a model showing eco-centric methods can also be economically viable.
